propositions.text: Applicant brought judicial review under s 72(1) IRPA of RAD decision.
propositions.quote: Fernando Ngandu (the Applicant) has brought an application for judicial review pursuant to s 72(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 (the IRPA) of a decision of the Refugee Appeal Division of the Immigration and Refugee Board (the RAD).

propositions.text: RAD upheld RPD decision that Applicant is neither Convention refugee nor person in need of protection.
propositions.quote: The RAD upheld the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) that the Applicant is neither a Convention refugee within the meaning of s 96 of the IRPA, nor a person in need of protection as defined in s 97(1) of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant brought judicial review of RAD decision upholding RPD finding Applicant not a Convention refugee or person in need of protection, court states.

propositions.text: Application for judicial review is allowed and matter remitted to RAD for re-determination by different panel.
propositions.quote: For the following reasons, the application for judicial review is allowed and the matter is remitted to the RAD for re-determination by a differently constituted panel.

paragraphs.summary: Court allows judicial review and remits matter to RAD for re-determination by different panel, court concludes.

propositions.text: Applicant is Angolan citizen who alleged torture by government agents due to protest participation and MSR membership.
propositions.quote: The Applicant is a citizen of Angola. He alleged before the RPD that he had been tortured by government agents because of his participation in protests against the government and because of his membership in a small youth group called the Movimiento Social Revolucionario (the MSR).

propositions.text: Applicant said he participated in November 2012 protest violently ended by police, was arrested, detained, tortured, hospitalized for head injury.
propositions.quote: The Applicant said that he had participated in a protest in November, 2012 which was violently ended by the police. He was arrested, detained and tortured, ultimately resulting in his hospitalisation for a head injury.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant, an Angolan citizen, alleged torture after protest participation and MSR membership, including arrest and hospitalization, court reports.

propositions.text: Applicant was released from hospital after two months via bribe; learned family missing after protests and MSR leader killed.
propositions.quote: After two months in the hospital, his mother bribed a doctor to release him. He then learned that his father and siblings were missing after their participation in anti-government protests, and a leader of the MSR had been killed.

propositions.text: Applicant distributed posters about government corruption; government agent fired at him; he left Angola and arrived in Canada May 2, 2013 to claim refugee status.
propositions.quote: In the months that followed, the Applicant distributed posters to raise awareness of government corruption. There was an incident where a government agent fired a gun at him, and the Applicant then decided to leave Angola. He arrived in Canada on May 2, 2013 and made a refugee claim.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant released from hospital by bribe, learned family missing, distributed posters, was shot at, fled to Canada and claimed refugee status, court states.

propositions.text: RPD dismissed claim for lack of credibility, finding Applicant never MSR member due to contradictory evidence and testimony.
propositions.quote: The RPD dismissed the Applicant’s claim on the ground that he lacked credibility. Based on a number of factors the RPD found that the Applicant had never been a member of the MSR: the leaders of the group identified in the documentary evidence were not the same as those identified by the Applicant in his testimony;

propositions.text: RPD found no evidence supporting two-month hospitalization claim and contradictions about when and where Applicant learned of family arrests.
propositions.quote: the Applicant had provided no evidence to support his claim of being hospitalised for two months; and the Applicant’s narrative and testimony were contradictory with respect to when and where he learned that his father and siblings had been arrested.

propositions.text: RPD drew negative inference from Applicant's inability to recall printer brand and contradictions about why he came to Canada instead of Brazil.
propositions.quote: The RPD also drew a negative inference from the Applicant’s inability to remember the brand name of the printer he used to produce the posters and from contradictions in the Applicant’s testimony regarding why he chose to come to Canada instead of making a refugee claim in Brazil.

paragraphs.summary: RPD dismissed claim for lack of credibility, finding Applicant not MSR member, no evidence of hospitalization, contradictions in testimony, court reports.

propositions.text: RAD confirmed RPD decision, refused new physician letter evidence as not material, found some RPD credibility errors but overall decision reasonable.
propositions.quote: The RAD confirmed the RPD’s decision. It refused to admit new evidence in the form of a letter from the Applicant’s physician regarding his cognitive impairment on the ground that the letter was not material. Applying the standard of reasonableness, the RAD concluded that the RPD had erred with respect to some of its credibility findings, but the decision as a whole was reasonable.

propositions.text: RAD found RPD satisfied procedural fairness requirements.
propositions.quote: The RAD also found that the RPD had satisfied the requirements of procedural fairness.

paragraphs.summary: RAD confirmed RPD decision, refused new evidence as not material, found some credibility errors but overall reasonable, and found procedural fairness, court reports.

propositions.text: Issues: RAD's refusal to admit physician letter; RAD's standard of review and reasonableness of credibility review; whether to certify question for appeal.
propositions.quote: This application for judicial review raises the following issues: A. Whether the RAD’s refusal to admit the letter from the Applicant’s physician as new evidence was reasonable; B. Whether the RAD’s review of the RPD’s findings of credibility was based on the correct standard of review and, if so, whether it was reasonable; and C. Whether a question should be certified for appeal.

paragraphs.summary: Court identifies issues: reasonableness of RAD refusing physician letter, correctness and reasonableness of RAD's credibility review, and certification for appeal.

propositions.text: RAD operational since Dec 2012; law unsettled on standard of review for RAD's own standard of review determination.
propositions.quote: The RAD became operational in December, 2012. It is a relatively new appellate tribunal, and the law is not yet settled regarding the standard of review to be applied by this Court to the RAD’s determination of its own standard of review.

propositions.text: Some Federal Court decisions apply correctness standard to RAD's interpretation of its appellate scope as question of general importance beyond RAD expertise.
propositions.quote: Some decisions of this Court have applied the standard of correctness, based on the assumption that the scope of the RAD’s appellate review, although a matter of interpretation by the RAD of its home statute, is a question of general importance to the legal system and is beyond the RAD’s expertise and experience (see, for example, Justice Phelan’s decision in Huruglica v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 799 at paras 25-34 [Huruglica] and Justice Barnes’ decision in Sow v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 295 at para 8 [Sow]).

paragraphs.summary: Court notes RAD is new and unsettled law on standard of review; some courts apply correctness standard to RAD's appellate scope interpretation, court explains.

propositions.text: Other Federal Court decisions apply reasonableness standard to RAD's determination of its own standard of review, finding it not a central legal question nor outside RAD expertise.
propositions.quote: By contrast, Justice Gagné in Akuffo v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 1063 at paras 17-26 [Akuffo] and Justice Martineau in Djossou v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 1080 at paras 13-37 [Djossou] found that this Court should apply the standard of reasonableness when considering the RAD’s determination of its own standard of review. They concluded that this is not a question of law of central importance to the legal system as a whole, nor does it fall outside the expertise of the RAD.

paragraphs.summary: Other courts apply reasonableness standard to RAD's self-determination of standard of review, finding it not central or outside RAD expertise, court explains.

propositions.text: Whether reasonableness or correctness applies to RAD's standard of review determination is not always outcome-determinative.
propositions.quote: Whether the Court applies the standard of reasonableness or correctness to the RAD’s identification of its own standard of review is not always determinative of the outcome of an application for judicial review before this Court (Djossou at para 37).

propositions.text: Justice Simon Noël in Yin v Canada advocates pragmatic approach pending Federal Court of Appeal resolution.
propositions.quote: As Justice Simon Noël remarked in Yin v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 1209 at para 33: […] the standard of review this Court should apply when reviewing the standard of intervention chosen by the RAD in its review of a RPD decision is undecided. As noted, this question is not determinative with regards to the case at bar. I therefore adhere to Justice Martineau’s approach in Djossou, supra at para 37, that until this question is resolved by the Federal Court of Appeal, a pragmatic approach should be used for the determination of the present judicial review.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes standard of review for RAD's self-review is undecided and not always determinative; pragmatic approach advised pending appeal court decision.

propositions.text: RAD errs if it applies judicial review standard when performing appellate functions.
propositions.quote: Nevertheless, this Court is unanimous that the RAD commits an error when it applies a judicial review standard while fulfilling its appellate functions (Djossou at paras 7, 37).

paragraphs.summary: Court states RAD errs if it applies judicial review standard during appellate functions.

propositions.text: RAD's application of law to facts and review of RPD credibility findings are reviewed on reasonableness standard.
propositions.quote: The RAD’s application of the law to the facts of the case and its consideration of the RPD’s credibility findings are both subject to review by this Court against a standard of reasonableness (Dunsmuir v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9; Nahal c Canada (Citoyenneté et Immigration), 2014 CF 1208 at para 25).

paragraphs.summary: Court states RAD's law application and credibility review are reviewed on reasonableness standard.

propositions.text: Standard of reasonableness applies to admissibility of new evidence before RAD.
propositions.quote: Finally, in Singh v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 1022 at paras 36-42 [Singh], Justice Gagné found that the standard of reasonableness also applies to questions regarding the admissibility of new evidence before the RAD.

paragraphs.summary: Court states standard of reasonableness applies to admissibility of new evidence before RAD.

propositions.text: Applicant objects to RAD's reliance on Raza FCA decision for new evidence admission criteria, as Raza concerned PRRA context.
propositions.quote: The Applicant objects to the RAD’s reliance on the Federal Court of Appeal’s decision in Raza v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FCA 385 in its determination of whether the new letter from the Applicant’s physician should have been admitted into evidence. Raza concerned the admission of new evidence in the context of a Pre-Removal Risk Assessment (PRRA).

propositions.text: Applicant argues RAD did not explain why PRRA criteria should apply to RAD appeals.
propositions.quote: The RAD did not explain why the criteria for admitting new evidence in the context of a PRRA should also apply to an appeal before the RAD.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues RAD wrongly relied on PRRA case Raza for new evidence criteria without explanation, applicant submits.

propositions.text: Applicant notes this Court held Raza criteria should not automatically apply to RAD new evidence admission.
propositions.quote: The Applicant notes that in Singh and in Khachatourian v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 182 at para 37 [Khachatourian], this Court held that the criteria identified in Raza should not automatically be applied to a determination of whether new evidence may be adduced before the RAD.

propositions.text: Applicant argues even if Raza criteria apply, RAD's materiality analysis of letter was unreasonable.
propositions.quote: In addition, the Applicant argues that even if this Court were to find that it was reasonable for the RAD to adopt the Raza criteria, the RAD’s application of these criteria was unreasonable because its analysis of the letter’s materiality was flawed.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues Raza criteria should not automatically apply to RAD new evidence and RAD's materiality analysis was unreasonable, applicant submits.

propositions.text: Respondent argues PRRA and RAD new evidence provisions are similar, so RAD reasonably applied Raza criteria.
propositions.quote: The Respondent points out that the language of the new evidence provisions in the PRRA context (s 113(a) of the IRPA) and in the RAD context (s 110(4) of the IRPA) are very similar, and it is therefore reasonable for the RAD to apply the Raza criteria to determine whether new evidence may be admitted before the RAD.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues PRRA and RAD new evidence provisions are similar, so RAD reasonably applied Raza criteria, respondent submits.

propositions.text: Section 110(4) IRPA limits RAD appeals to evidence arising after claim rejection or not reasonably available then.
propositions.quote: With respect to an appeal before the RAD, s 110(4) of the IRPA provides as follows: (4) On appeal, the person who is the subject of the appeal may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection.

paragraphs.summary: Court states s 110(4) IRPA limits RAD appeals to evidence arising after claim rejection or not reasonably available then.

propositions.text: Section 113(a) IRPA limits PRRA applicants to new evidence arising after rejection or not reasonably available then.
propositions.quote: In the context of a PRRA, s 113(a) of the IRPA provides as follows: (a) an applicant whose claim to refugee protection has been rejected may present only new evidence that arose after the rejection or was not reasonably available, or that the applicant could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection;

paragraphs.summary: Court states s 113(a) IRPA limits PRRA applicants to new evidence arising after rejection or not reasonably available then.

propositions.text: PRRA officer is not quasi-judicial or appellate; must defer to RPD unless new evidence arises; PRRA is last chance to assess new risks before removal.
propositions.quote: A PRRA officer is not a quasi-judicial body, nor does he or she have an appellate function when faced with a RPD decision. The PRRA officer is an employee of the Minister, acting within his or her employer’s discretion (insofar as it is circumscribed by the Act and the Regulations). The PRRA officer must give deference to the RPD’s determination of the claim, to the extent that the facts remain unchanged from the time it had rendered its decision. Instead, the PRRA officer is specifically looking as to whether new evidence has come to life since the RPD’s rejection of the claim for determining a risk of persecution, a danger of torture, a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment. The underlying rationale for paragraph 113(a) of the Act is not appellate in nature but rather to assure the claimant has a last chance to have any new risks of refoulement (not previously assessed by the RPD) assessed before removal can take place.

paragraphs.summary: Court explains PRRA officer is not appellate, defers to RPD, and assesses new risks before removal, per prior authority.

propositions.text: RAD is quasi-judicial appellate body conducting full fact-based appeals; evidence rules applied flexibly due to refugee claim timelines.
propositions.quote: This may be contrasted with the RAD, which is a quasi-judicial appellate body that is intended by Parliament to conduct a “full fact-based appeal” of decisions of the RPD. A “full fact-based appeal” requires that the rules of evidence be applied with a measure of flexibility, especially given the strict timelines faced by refugee claimants (Singh at paras 53-56; Khachatourian at para 37).

paragraphs.summary: Court explains RAD is quasi-judicial appellate body conducting full fact-based appeals with flexible evidence rules due to refugee timelines.

propositions.text: RAD accepted the physician's letter as new, credible and relevant but not material due to lack of neurologist qualification
propositions.quote: the RAD accepted that the letter from the Applicant’s physician was new, credible and relevant, but found that it was not material because the physician was not a qualified neurologist

propositions.text: RAD reasoned physician would have referred Applicant to neurologist if cognitive decline suspected
propositions.quote: The RAD reasoned that if the physician suspected that the Applicant’s cognitive functioning was deteriorating, then he would have referred him to a neurologist for assessment.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD accepted the physician's letter as new and credible but not material, reasoning the physician would have referred the Applicant to a neurologist if needed.

propositions.text: RAD erred applying Raza criteria to admit new physician's letter
propositions.quote: I conclude that the RAD erred in applying the Raza criteria to its determination of whether to admit the new letter from the Applicant’s physician.

propositions.text: Court cannot say if a more flexible approach would have led to admitting the letter or changed outcome
propositions.quote: I am unable to say whether a more flexible approach would have caused the RAD to admit the physician’s letter into evidence, nor whether this would have enabled the Applicant to obtain an oral hearing or given him an opportunity to explain the inconsistencies in his testimony

propositions.text: Application for judicial review must be allowed due to uncertainty about impact of letter admission
propositions.quote: Because I am unable to conclude whether the RAD’s decision would have been different if the more recent letter from the physician had been admitted, the application for judicial review must be allowed.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RAD erred applying Raza criteria and allows judicial review because it cannot determine if admitting the letter would have changed the decision.

propositions.text: RAD erred by reviewing RPD decision as if conducting judicial review
propositions.quote: The Applicant argues that the RAD erred by assessing the RPD’s decision as if it were conducting an application for judicial review.

propositions.text: RAD is specialized tribunal with more expertise than RPD and can issue precedential decisions
propositions.quote: The RAD is a specialized tribunal that hears appeals from the RPD, whose members are presumed to have less expertise than members of the RAD. In addition, the RAD has the power to issue decisions with precedential value

propositions.text: RAD can consider fact, law, mixed questions, hold oral hearings on new credibility evidence, and substitute decisions
propositions.quote: and to consider questions of fact, law, or mixed fact and law. The RAD may hold an oral hearing when there is new evidence that relates to a question of credibility. Finally, the RAD has the power not only to set aside a decision of the RPD, but also to substitute its own decision.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the RAD erred by reviewing the RPD decision like a judicial review, despite RAD's broader powers and expertise.

propositions.text: Court ruled RAD must not apply judicial review standard on appeal and RAD failed to use recognized approaches
propositions.quote: The Applicant points out that this Court has ruled that the RAD must not apply the standard of judicial review when conducting an appeal, and in this case the RAD did not adopt any of the approaches that have been recognized by this Court as appropriate.

propositions.text: Applicant was denied right to meaningful appeal
propositions.quote: Accordingly, the Applicant was denied his right to a meaningful appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the RAD wrongly applied judicial review standard and denied him a meaningful appeal.

propositions.text: RAD wrongly found RPD's adverse credibility finding reasonable about Applicant's explanation of MSR leader's death
propositions.quote: The Applicant also disputes the RAD’s assessment of the RPD’s credibility findings. The RAD concluded that it was reasonable for the RPD to draw an adverse finding of credibility from the Applicant’s unsatisfactory explanation of how he learned of the death of one of the MSR’s leaders.

propositions.text: RPD accepted translation error and found discrepancy more apparent than real
propositions.quote: contrary to the RAD’s finding, the RPD in fact accepted that there had been an error of translation, and concluded that the discrepancy was “more apparent than real.”

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant disputes RAD's finding that RPD's adverse credibility finding was reasonable; RPD accepted a translation error and found discrepancy apparent.

propositions.text: RAD properly applied reasonableness standard and owes deference to RPD's credibility findings
propositions.quote: The Respondent says that it was open to the RAD to apply the standard of reasonableness when reviewing the RPD’s findings of credibility, because the RAD owes deference to the RPD in this regard.

propositions.text: Appeals before RAD usually in writing; RAD accepts new evidence and holds hearings only in limited circumstances
propositions.quote: Appeals before the RAD are usually conducted in writing, and the RAD accepts new evidence and holds hearings only in limited circumstances.

propositions.text: RPD plays primary role in refugee determination and is best placed to assess evidence from witness testimony
propositions.quote: According to the Respondent, the RPD “plays the primary role in the refugee determination process”. The RPD is in the best position to assess the evidence, because it sees and hears witnesses’ testimony.

propositions.text: Court found RAD owes deference to RPD credibility findings based on witness testimony (Allalou)
propositions.quote: This Court has found that the RAD owes deference to the RPD’s credibility findings when they are based on witnesses’ testimony (Allalou v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 1084 at paras 17-20 [Allalou]).

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent argues RAD properly applied reasonableness standard and owes deference to RPD's credibility findings based on witness testimony.

propositions.text: Court erred in Huruglica and similar cases by saying RAD owes no deference to RPD factual findings not based on witness testimony
propositions.quote: The Respondent maintains that this Court erred in Huruglica and the cases that have followed it insofar as these stand for the proposition that the RAD owes no deference to factual findings of the RPD that are not dependent on witness testimony.

propositions.text: These cases failed to consider importance of hearing process giving RPD deeper engagement with evidence
propositions.quote: According to the Respondent, these cases “did not properly take into account the importance of the hearing process which allows the RPD to have a deeper engagement with the entire evidentiary record.”

propositions.text: RAD may have equal expertise on country reports but independent review conflicts with efficient appeal goal
propositions.quote: The Respondent recognizes that the RAD “may have equal expertise” with respect to assessing country condition reports, but argues that requiring the RAD to conduct an independent review is incompatible with the legislative objective of creating an efficient and effective appeal mechanism.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent argues the Court erred in denying RAD deference to RPD factual findings not based on testimony and that independent review conflicts with efficient appeals.

propositions.text: RAD's application of reasonableness standard to RPD findings is defensible
propositions.quote: The Respondent therefore defends the RAD’s application of the reasonableness standard to its review of the RPD’s decision.

propositions.text: Alternatively, appellate standard of overriding and palpable error applies and is equivalent to reasonableness
propositions.quote: Alternatively, the Respondent asserts that the proper standard of review for questions of fact is the appellate standard of overriding and palpable error. In this case, applying that standard produces the same result since it is functionally equivalent to the standard of reasonableness (HL v Canada (Attorney General), 2005 SCC 25 at para 110).

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent defends RAD's reasonableness standard application or alternatively the appellate standard of overriding and palpable error.

propositions.text: RAD's misunderstanding of discrepancy in Applicant's testimony was not central as other credibility conclusions unaffected
propositions.quote: Finally, the Respondent says that the RAD’s misunderstanding of the apparent discrepancy in the Applicant’s testimony about how he learned of the death of a leader of the MSR was not central to its decision, since many other conclusions regarding his credibility were not affected by this error.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent argues RAD's error about the Applicant's testimony discrepancy was not central to its decision.

propositions.text: Court agrees with Applicant that RAD erred applying reasonableness standard to RPD factual findings
propositions.quote: Despite the Respondent’s able arguments, I find myself in agreement with the Applicant. This Court has ruled repeatedly that the RAD commits an error when it applies the standard of reasonableness to its review of the RPD’s factual findings (Djossou at paras 6 and 7).

paragraphs.summary: The Court agrees with the Applicant that the RAD erred by applying the reasonableness standard to RPD factual findings.

propositions.text: Deference is owed to RPD credibility assessments based on witness testimony due to advantage of seeing and hearing witnesses
propositions.quote: I acknowledge that the RAD owes deference to an assessment of credibility by the RPD that is based on witness testimony. As the Supreme Court of Canada observed in R v NS, 2012 SCC 72 at para 25: It is a settled axiom of appellate review that deference should be shown to the trier of fact on issues of credibility because trial judges (and juries) have the “overwhelming advantage” of seeing and hearing the witness

paragraphs.summary: The Court states deference is owed to RPD credibility assessments based on witness testimony due to their advantage in seeing and hearing witnesses.

propositions.text: Most judges hold RAD owes deference only when witness credibility is critical or RPD has particular advantage
propositions.quote: Most judges of this Court have held that, because the RAD is a specialized tribunal which conducts a “full fact-based appeal”, it owes deference to the RPD only when a witness’ credibility is critical or determinative or when the RPD enjoys a particular advantage

propositions.text: RAD and RPD are equally positioned to assess factual findings not dependent on testimony
propositions.quote: From the perspective of establishing facts... one may reasonably ask whether a RAD member is in just as good a position as a RPD member to reassess the evidence in the record where it is alleged on appeal that the RPD erred in its assessment of the evidence as a whole

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds most judges hold RAD owes deference only when witness credibility is critical; otherwise RAD and RPD are equally positioned to assess facts.

propositions.text: Most judges conclude RAD must conduct independent assessment of evidence including credibility questions
propositions.quote: Most judges of this Court have concluded that the RAD must conduct its own independent assessment of the evidence (Iyamuremye... Huruglica... Djossou). The RAD’s obligation extends to questions of credibility.

paragraphs.summary: Most judges conclude RAD must independently assess evidence and credibility questions on appeal.

propositions.text: Some decisions uphold RAD's reasonableness standard on credibility only if RAD conducted independent assessment
propositions.quote: this Court will uphold the RAD’s application of the reasonableness standard to the RPD’s findings of credibility only when it is clear that the RAD has in fact conducted its own assessment of the evidence.

propositions.text: In pure credibility cases, the key is whether RAD conducted independent assessment, not which standard applied
propositions.quote: in cases involving findings of pure credibility, the point is not which standard was applied but rather “whether the RAD conducted an independent assessment of the evidence as a whole.”

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds RAD's reasonableness standard on credibility is upheld only if RAD independently assessed evidence; independent assessment is key.

propositions.text: Respondent argues independent assessment by RAD requires reading thousands of pages, conflicting with efficient appeal goal
propositions.quote: The Respondent cautions that in order to conduct an independent assessment of the evidence the RAD member would have to read “thousands of pages of documents”, and argues that this would be incompatible with the legislative goal of creating an efficient appeal system.

propositions.text: RAD's power to substitute decisions and Parliament's intent require full fact-based appeal and independent assessment
propositions.quote: this must be reconciled with the RAD’s power to substitute its own determination for that of the RPD and Parliament’s intention to provide a “full fact-based appeal” (Huruglica at para 40).

propositions.text: Substituting a decision without assessing evidence is inconsistent with IRPA's purpose
propositions.quote: “the idea that the RAD may substitute an impugned decision by a determination that should have been rendered without first assessing the evidence is inconsistent with the purpose of the IRPA” (Triastcin v Canada... at para 25).

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent argues independent assessment is burdensome; the Court says RAD's substitution power and IRPA require full fact-based appeal and evidence assessment.

propositions.text: RAD erred by reviewing RPD credibility findings under reasonableness standard and did not consistently conduct independent assessment
propositions.quote: In this case, the RAD was wrong to review the RPD’s findings of credibility against the standard of reasonableness. The RAD’s decision does not permit this Court to conclude that it consistently conducted an independent assessment of the evidence.

propositions.text: RAD independently concluded on one RPD error but failed to independently assess other adverse credibility findings
propositions.quote: The RAD reached an independent conclusion with respect to the RPD’s erroneous finding of a contradiction... However, the RAD did not conduct an independent assessment of the RPD’s adverse credibility finding regarding the Applicant’s allegations of participation in protests, detention and torture.

propositions.text: RAD incorrectly tried to supplement incomplete RPD reasons citing Newfoundland Nurses' Union case
propositions.quote: Rather than evaluating the evidence as a whole, the RAD first attempted to supplement the incomplete reasons of the RPD, incorrectly citing Newfoundland and Labrador Nurses' Union v Newfoundland and Labrador (Treasury Board), 2011 SCC 62 as its authority for doing so.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds RAD erred applying reasonableness standard and failed to consistently independently assess RPD credibility findings, wrongly citing precedent.

propositions.text: RAD misapprehended RPD's conclusion on discrepancy in Applicant's testimony, affecting overall reasonableness finding
propositions.quote: The RAD’s misapprehension of the RPD’s conclusion regarding the “more apparent than real” contradiction... provides another basis for allowing the application for judicial review.

propositions.text: If RAD had not misapprehended, it might have found RPD decision unreasonable overall
propositions.quote: If the RAD had not misapprehended the RPD’s determination on this question of credibility, this may have shifted the balance and caused the RAD to conclude that the RPD’s decision as a whole was unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds RAD misapprehended RPD's conclusion on a testimony discrepancy, possibly affecting its overall reasonableness finding.

propositions.text: Application for judicial review is allowed
propositions.quote: The application for judicial review is therefore allowed.

paragraphs.summary: The Court allows the application for judicial review.

propositions.text: Two determinative issues have been certified for appeal previously
propositions.quote: Two of three determinative issues in this application for judicial review have previously been certified for appeal.

propositions.text: No questions are certified for appeal as Applicant succeeded and issues will be decided in other cases
propositions.quote: I do not find it necessary to certify questions for appeal in this case.

paragraphs.summary: The Court notes two issues are already certified for appeal and declines to certify questions here as Applicant succeeded.
